notes:
I've arranged these notes verse by verse. For each one I give the traditional reading first, then where commentators differ, then other views. After each point I name the source and give its URL. A few gaps:

- I found no teaching from Methodist sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Pentecostal sites, Lutheran sites or oca.org. The only Methodist voice is Adam Clarke, quoted on StudyLight and Blue Letter Bible, and the only Lutheran note is a second-hand mention of how Luther translated two words.
- I found nothing from prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teachers on this psalm, so that section is left out.
- I couldn't open Spurgeon's full *Treasury of David* page, so I only used the parts that appeared in search results.

**Setting and title**
- Bible Hub's study notes say the psalm was given to the choir leader. That means a private grief was brought into the people's shared worship. https://biblehub.com/psalms/42-1.htm
- Guzik says the sons of Korah were Levites. They survived the judgment on Korah's rebellion and may have become known for praise out of gratitude for that mercy. This psalm opens Book Two of the Psalms. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-42/
- Who wrote it, and when? GotQuestions thinks the sons of Korah were travelling with David when Absalom drove him out of Jerusalem. https://www.gotquestions.org/deep-calls-to-deep.html. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) suggests the writer was a Levite singer in exile with David. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_042.cfm. Utley's notes at Bible.org report the NASB Study Bible's suggestion that the writer was a Korahite Levite taken captive by Syria. Utley himself thinks the people taunting him were his captors. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-42
- Bible Hub notes that Psalm 43 has the same refrain, so the two psalms were probably one unit. https://biblehub.com/psalms/42.htm

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** Spurgeon says David, shut out from public worship, needed fellowship with God the way a stag needs water. To him it was a necessity, not a luxury. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-1.htm
- Gill pictures the deer as hot or hunted by dogs. The psalmist, likewise, was persecuted and cut off from worship, which made him long for fellowship with God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-1.htm
- **Deer, or female deer?** Barnes says "deer" is a masculine word but its verb is feminine, so it means a female deer (a hind). He adds that the Hebrew word stresses longing more than panting. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-1.htm. The Expositor's Bible (Maclaren) says "soul" is also feminine in Hebrew, and the timid hind is a fitting picture of the soul. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-42.html
- **Drought or hunt?** Commentators disagree about what made the deer thirsty. Benson pictures a hunted animal almost spent. The Cambridge Bible points to Joel 1:20 and says the picture comes from drought, not the chase. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-1.htm
- **Translation note:** Barnes reports that Luther rendered the verb "cries." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-1.htm
- **Catholic/patristic reading:** Augustine says the speaker is "ourselves" and also the Church, Christ's one Body. He says the psalm was usually sung for people preparing for baptism, so they would long for the fountain of forgiveness. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801042.htm
- Augustine also uses an old belief that deer kill snakes and then grow thirstier. He reads the snakes as our vices: kill them and you will thirst more for God. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801042.htm

**v. 2**
- Benson says thirst is more urgent than hunger. "The living God" is the everlasting spring of life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-1.htm
- Guzik gives three senses of "living God": He has life in Himself, He gives life, and He is unlike the dead gods of the nations. Quoting Poole, he says "appear before God" means appearing where God's presence was specially known in public worship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-42/
- Spurgeon says anyone who loves the Lord loves the gatherings where He is worshipped. David did not settle for private worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-1.htm
- Augustine reads the thirst as a pilgrim's longing that will be satisfied only on arrival before God. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.XLII.html

**v. 3**
- Guzik says the tears show both his grief and his sense that God was far away. Quoting Boice, he says the taunt did not deny that God exists. It meant God had abandoned him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-42/
- Spurgeon says the taunt hurt because it attacked God's faithfulness. He suggests it may allude to Shimei mocking David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-1.htm
- Augustine notes the text says tears were his "food," not his "drink," so he still thirsted for the brooks. A pagan can point to the sun as his god, but the believer's God cannot be seen with bodily eyes. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801042.htm
- Harold Kim (The Gospel Coalition) points out that the psalmist mentions tears but no proper eating or sleep. He cites Lloyd-Jones's warning that body and soul affect each other. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/pastor-quit-preach-yourself/

**v. 4**
- Guzik says remembering joyful festival crowds at God's house made the present sadder. Quoting Poole, he says he poured out his soul privately so his enemies could not gloat. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-42/
- Boice (quoted at Precept Austin) says memory can be used rightly: recalling what God did before encourages trust that He will act again. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_425_commentary
- Augustine reads God's house as the faithful themselves, God's tabernacle on earth, and as a heavenly festival heard faintly by the heart. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801042.htm

**v. 5**
- **Traditional reading:** Spurgeon says the psalmist talks to himself as if he were two men, his faith reasoning with his fears. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_425_commentary
- Guzik says he refused simply to give in to his feelings. Quoting Poole, "the help of His countenance" is literally "the salvations of His face." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-42/
- **Reformed and Baptist use of Lloyd-Jones:** Lloyd-Jones's book *Spiritual Depression* came from sermons on this psalm. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/a-word-to-self. John Piper (Desiring God) calls this "preaching to yourself," with God's future grace as the main argument. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/preach-to-yourself. Ligonier's devotional adds a balance: the help must come from outside ourselves, in the gospel. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/a-word-to-self
- **Is being downcast a sin?** Teachers differ, though not neatly by church tradition:
  - A Matthew Henry comment on Bible Hub says being cast down comes from unbelief and should be resisted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-1.htm
  - Spurgeon calls it "faithless fainting." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps042.cfm
  - Harold Kim (TGC) stresses that the psalm describes no sin. He compares the psalmist's state to a loss of spiritual senses with no moral failure. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/pastor-quit-preach-yourself/
- **Hebrew words:** Bible Hub notes that "hope" (yachal) means tense, expectant waiting. https://biblehub.com/psalms/42.htm. The NET Bible translates "Wait for God!" https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_425_commentary

**v. 6**
- **Traditional reading:** Calvin says he did not try to forget God in his trouble. Though exiled, he turned to God as his physician. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/42-6.html
- Matthew Henry says that wherever he was driven, he took his faith with him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/42-6.html
- Spurgeon sees him recalling past times of fellowship with God at these places. He also allows that David may mean any place can be holy where God is. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-6.htm
- **What is Mizar?** Views vary:
  - JFB thinks the name "little hill" may show contempt for the place of exile. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_042.cfm
  - Bishop Horsley (cited by Clarke) took the "little hill" to be Zion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-42.html. Ellicott rejects that reading, since Hebrew poetry exalted Zion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-6.htm
  - Gill reports Jewish readings that take it as Sinai. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-6.htm
  - Augustine reads "little hill" as a lesson in humility. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801042.htm
- **NET Bible notes:** "remember" here stands for prayer. The place is the upper Jordan. Mizar is probably a real mountain in the Hermon area, named only here. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/b/o/passage.php?passage=Psa+42:6-8&mode=print

**v. 7**
- **Traditional reading:** Benson and Poole say one trouble comes right after another, as if called by the first. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-7.htm
- Gill says they are "His" waves because God sends, orders and overrules them for His people's good. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-7.htm
- Guzik sees outer and inner trouble colliding. Yet the waterfalls are God's, so He is there and has measured the trouble. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-42/
- **God's wrath, or God's mercy?** Calvin says when God's anger is kindled, "depth will call unto depth," and readers should take God's warnings seriously. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/42-7.html. Matthew Henry likewise says David saw his troubles as coming from God's wrath. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/42-7.html. In contrast, Bible Hub's article quotes Augustine: human misery calls to the depth of God's compassion. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Deep_calls_to_deep_in_Ps_42_7.htm. GotQuestions gives both the "waves of trouble" reading and the "deep need calls to God's depth" reading. https://www.gotquestions.org/deep-calls-to-deep.html
- Spurgeon's sermon applies the verse to suffering met by God's grace, and to the depth of sin met by Christ's atonement. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/deep-calleth-unto-deep/
- **Methodist voice (Clarke):** One wave of sorrow drives on another, and the Hebrew itself has a dismal sound. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/42-7.html
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible):** "Deep" here probably means mountain streams near Hermon, pictured as calling to each other. The psalmist imagines himself swept under by the current. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/b/o/passage.php?passage=Psa+42:6-8&mode=print. The Cambridge Bible notes that Jonah 2:3 borrows this line. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-7.htm

**v. 8**
- JFB says he still trusts in a steady flow of God's mercy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_042.cfm
- Matthew Henry says that after the storm comes calm, and that hope held him up. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/42-7.html
- NET Bible note: here the psalmist switches from "God" to the personal name Yahweh ("the LORD") as he speaks of God's loyal love. A few manuscripts read "praise" instead of "prayer." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/b/o/passage.php?passage=Psa+42:6-8&mode=print
- Desiring God suggests this psalm may itself be that night-time prayer-song. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/when-depression-descends-do-the-next-thing

**v. 9**
- JFB says he composes a prayer to himself out of his distress, made worse by his enemies' taunts. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_042.cfm
- An older note in Spurgeon's *Treasury* links "God my Rock" to David the fugitive sheltering among rocks and caves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/42-6.htm
- Guzik lists God's seemingly slow response as one of the reasons for discouragement. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-42/

**v. 10**
- JFB calls the taunts cruel "infidel suggestions." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_042.cfm
- Boice (at Precept Austin) says the line is repeated because it hurt so much. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm_425_commentary
- Bible Hub links the taunt to the mockers at the cross (Matthew 27:43). https://biblehub.com/psalms/42.htm

**v. 11**
- JFB says he scolds himself again. "Health of my countenance" means God drives the clouds of sorrow from his face. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_042.cfm
- Guzik says the repeated refrain shows hope is an ongoing conversation with oneself, not a one-time decision. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-42/
- Clarke says there is no reason to despair, because God will free the captives. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-42.html
- Kim (TGC) says the repetition reflects patience, taking time with God and with oneself. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/pastor-quit-preach-yourself/

**Other views on the whole psalm**
- **Dispensational reading:** Kingcomments (Brethren) reads Psalms 42–43 prophetically about a faithful Jewish remnant suffering under the Antichrist in the end times. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/psalms-42.html
- **Augustine on the title:** He takes "Korah" to stand for Calvary. So the "sons of Korah" are Christians redeemed by Christ's cross. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801042.htm
